title: Improving Cities from Space: Geospatial Innovations in North and Central Asia
content:
By Kareff Rafisura, Ladislav Charouz and Elena A. Pronina*

BANGKOK | 26 October 2026 (IDN) — Cities in North and Central Asia are growing quickly, bringing them face to face with the interlinked challenges of rapid urbanisation, rising population density, and heightened vulnerability to disaster and climate risks. World Cities Day is a good opportunity to consider these challenges and how geospatial technologies can help address them.

Following up on an earlier ESCAP article about satellite-enabled urban solutions in East and North-East Asia, this piece turns to North and Central Asia, where governments are applying geospatial technologies and satellite data across a growing range of areas – from monitoring and urban planning to tracking accessibility.

Disaster and climate resilience is one such area. Kazakhstan, for example, uses a satellite monitoring system, JerScan, to keep track of ageing infrastructure, reducing the need for physical field inspections.

title: EEPA reports on clashes erupt in Ethiopia-Kenya border town
content:
BRUSSELS | 26 October 2026 (IDN | EEPA) — The following are the situation reports on the situation in Ethiopia, the situation in Sudan, the regional and international situation, clashes erupt in Ethiopia-Kenya border town, drone strikes cause power outage in White Nile, UK sanctions RSF and SAF officials

  • Tension escalated in the town of Moyale between leaders of Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regions on 18 October amid allegations of the unauthorized raising of the Somali regional flag by its leaders. Moyale is jointly administered by the Somali and Oromia regions. 
  • Over 14,000 people have been displaced in the Moyale area since the fighting broke out on 22 October, with nine people killed between 22 and 23 October. 
  • Thousands of Ethiopian nationals have crossed the border into Kenya in order to escape fighting in Moyale. The Kenya Red Cross has begun providing displaced individuals with first aid essentials, while Kenya Defence Forces troops have been moved to the border with Ethiopia since tensions escalated. 
  • The ongoing clashes in Moyale have now spread to three additional districts in South Oromia, including  Gumi Eldallo, Wachile, and Arero.

title: Returns on Ethics: A New Compass for Global Finance in an Age of Debt and Inequality
content:
By Jayasri Priyalal*

SINGAPORE | 24 October 2026 (IDN) — As the world moves closer to the 2030 deadline for achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), a troubling reality is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore.

Global wealth continues to expand, financial markets reach record valuations, and technological innovation accelerates at an unprecedented pace. Yet millions of people are falling behind, public services are under strain, and environmental degradation continues unabated. The question confronting policymakers is no longer whether the global economic model is under stress, but whether the metrics guiding that model remain fit for purpose.

title: The Old Bus Was an Adventure. Will the New One Last?
content:
A schoolboy commuter’s memories of Sri Lanka in the 1980s and 90s — and a look at the country’s new Metro Bus service.

By Feroz Deen*

COLOMBO | 24 October 2026 (IDN) — In the 1980s and 90s, catching a bus in Sri Lanka was an adventure. Getting on was a struggle, never mind getting a seat. As teenagers, hanging on the footboard of a bus was the equivalent of a Sathutu Uyana jet ride at Viharamahadevi Park — the only theme park many Sri Lankan kids had access to back then.

As I grew older, I realised how dangerous — and potentially fatal — riding on the footboard could be. I would never encourage anyone to do it today.

On the bus, passengers smoked despite signs prohibiting it. It was a time when smoking was taken much more lightly. I remember a friend of mine, arrogant as only a teenager can be, telling off an older man for lighting up. Nobody was quite sure who had won.

On the way home from Wesley College, Borella Junction was the big stop. The driver wouldn’t move until he had collected his quota of passengers. And if another bus tried to overtake, the Grand Prix would begin.

title: Renewing the Momentum for Rights-based Poverty Reduction in Asia and the Pacific
content:
By Katinka Weinberger and Mizuho Okimoto-Kaewtathip*

BANGKOK | 23 October 2026 (IDN) — Eradicating poverty in all its forms is one of the most pressing development challenges across Asia and the Pacific. While the region has made remarkable progress in reducing poverty over recent decades, multiple and overlapping crises have exposed the fragility of these achievements and highlighted how easily gains can be reversed.

Poverty is a dynamic phenomenon shaped by structural drivers that reinforce vulnerability and widen inequalities across societies and generations. Economic growth has been the main driver of poverty reduction in the region, but inequality has weakened its impact and undermined the full benefits of this progress. Inequalities slow economic progress and trap many countries in chronic poverty patterns that can persist across generations.

title: Africa Aims to Transform The Continent Inspired By Asia’s Rise
content:
By Kalinga Seneviratne

BANGKOK, Thailand | 21 October 2026 (IDN) — The IMF-World Bank annual meeting returned to Bangkok last week (12 to 18 October) after more than three decades, with nervous Thai authorities going to great lengths to prevent civil society protests from disrupting it.

Inside Bangkok’s convention centre, World Bank’s turbaned American-Sikh President Ajay Banga led a charm offensive to convince the world that the Bank is transforming the development model of previous generations into one that addresses the expectations of equality among nations. He also talked about building models that develop local industries, create local jobs, and keep the value of natural resources at home. He also launched a Philanthropy Hub in Bangkok, which the Bank says will push it toward more partnerships with a variety of stakeholders.

title: Why Doesn’t the US Implement Its Treaties?
content:
By Jonathan Power

LUND, Sweden | 21 October 2026 (IDN) – The US Senate—usually the Republican members—rejects multilateral treaties as if it were a sport. Others it rejects through inaction—the Law of the Sea Treaty, for example, negotiated under President Jimmy Carter and fruitlessly pushed for ratification by every president since. Republicans justify their blocking tactics by arguing that such treaties threaten sovereignty.

However, after almighty struggles—it takes only one third of the Senate to block a treaty—the important nuclear arms treaties with the Soviet Union and Russia were ratified. So was the Convention against Torture, which Republican President Ronald Reagan successfully fought for but which President George Bush junior illegally ignored, without a word of protest from Congress or most of the media. His vice-president, Dick Cheney, became torturer-in-chief and should have been arrested by the incoming Obama Administration. But Obama, wanting a peaceful life with Congress for the sake of future legislation, decided not to prosecute the torturers.

In October 2013, Syria joined the Chemical Weapons Treaty that the US has long been a party to.

title: Israel’s Fateful Election: A Nation On The Brink
content:
Israel’s next election will decide far more than who governs. It will help determine whether the country can reclaim its democratic foundations, restore its international standing, and fulfil its founding promise—or continue down a path that endangers the very future its leaders claim to defend.

By Alon Ben-Meir*

NEW YORK | 20 October 2026 (IDN) — Hardly any election in Israel’s history has carried such profound consequences. Israelis will face a choice that reaches far beyond party allegiance: what kind of country will they leave their children? After 7 October and three years of devastating wars, Israel’s security, democratic character, and promise as a Jewish homeland demand an unsparing national reckoning—one that confronts democratic erosion through judicial subversion, institutional capture, press intimidation, dissent suppression, minority disenfranchisement, unchecked executive power, perpetual warfare, and isolation.

title: Decoding Pro-Israel Buzzwords in a Time of Genocide
content:
By Norman Solomon*

SAN FRANCISCO | 20 October 2026 (IDN) — Nearly two years ago, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International released in-depth reports documenting that Israel had committed genocide in Gaza. Months later, Israeli human rights groups did likewise. Support for Israel has declined steeply among Americans, but its defenders continue to maintain a siege of buzzwords against Palestinian rights.

As historian Rashid Khalidi emphasized in his book Brokers of Deceit: How the U.S. Has Undermined Peace in the Middle East, “language matters.” Standard terms and tropes “are the essential building blocks of a lofty and solid edifice of denial of an entire narrative, of the existence of an entire people, which is basic to the affirmation of a formidable counterreality.”

Prominent groups, notably the Anti-Defamation League, the American Jewish Committee, AIPAC and Christians United for Israel – along with allies in Congress, the Executive Branch and the punditocracy – rely on the same buzzwords to defame critics of Israel and deny its systematic crimes against Palestinian people. title: OPINION: Protecting the Sacred City of Anuradhapura
content:
By Dr. Asoka Bandarage*

COLOMBO. Sri Lanka | 27 October 2026 (IDN) — Buddhism was first introduced to Sri Lanka in Anuradhapura in the 3rd century BCE by Arahant Mahinda, the son of the Indian Emperor Asoka. For nearly 1500 years, Anuradhapura remained Sri Lanka’s capital and the intellectual and spiritual centre of Theravada Buddhism in Asia. The Anuradhapura civilisation achieved unmatched advances in architecture, engineering and urban planning, still evident in its monumental stupas, monasteries, palaces and sophisticated hydraulic and agricultural systems.

Buddhism was gradually assimilated into Hinduism and had disappeared from India by the 12th century CE. The Chola invasion from India and the sacking and conquest in 1017 CE dealt a heavy blow to Buddhist civilisation, ending Anuradhapura’s role as the island’s political capital. The sacred city has continued to face attacks, including the LTTE massacre of 146 devotees at the Sri Maha Bodhi on Vesak full moon, 14 May 1985. Yet Anuradhapura has survived as one of the world’s oldest continuously inhabited cities and as a sacred site that has attracted Buddhist pilgrims over the centuries.

title: 40 years in the spirit of Assisi
content:
By Benoit Lannoo*

ASSISI. Italy | 27 October 2026 (IDN) — Today, it has been exactly forty years since John Paul II brought together different religions in Assisi for the first time for an interreligious prayer for peace.

In his recently published book (in Italian, French and German) entitled Assisi – The Origins of a Spiritual Globalization, the Roman historian Andrea Riccardi, founder of the Community of Sant’Egidio, points out that even the “iconographic material of Assisi 1986” remains important. He is referring to the emblematic photo of St. Pope John Paul II surrounded by the Dalai Lama and a large number of other leaders of Churches and religions, sitting next to each other on small chairs all of the same size in the square in front of the lower basilica of St. Francis in Assisi. They had just prayed for peace at the same time but all in their tradition and customs.

Alas, for today’s closing ceremony of the 40th Meeting in the spirit of Assisi, the current pope will not be physically present since the doctors have advised him not to travel by helicopter. But Leo XIV will send a message to the festive assembly.
